intro: Plastic surgeons treat wounds every day, yet "wound" means different things in operative notes, registries and trials. A diabetic foot ulcer, an irradiated scalp defect and a traumatic leg wound share that label but differ in biology, reconstruction and expected outcome. Free text cannot record these differences in a form a computer can use, so studies are hard to compare and decision support hard to build. We asked whether the distinctions surgeons already make can be written down as a model a computer can check.
methods: We built one for wounds: a hierarchy in which every concept is a kind of something more general, with explicit rules linking them. Concepts and relations were gathered from 6,029 published wound abstracts by a pipeline we built ourselves, combining large language models with Formal Concept Analysis, a mathematical method that groups concepts by shared properties. Nothing was accepted on an automatic proposal alone: a human reviewer ruled on every placement, anything unjustified was dropped, and a relation became a rule only where it held for every example.
results: The model grew from 489 to 3,535 concepts; a further 4,104 candidates were left out as unverified. Formal Concept Analysis added nothing: wound properties are reported too sparsely to form meaningful groups. Automated logical checking found no self-contradictory concept, either alone or together with the established biomedical vocabularies it draws on, some 9,200 concepts in all. Of 73 clinical questions agreed in advance, all 49 within the intended scope were answered correctly; the other 24 were declared outside it.
conclusion: Wound terminology can be made precise enough for a computer without being loosened to fit: most of what was extracted was refused, and what remains is consistent. This gives reconstructive surgery a shared, machine-readable vocabulary for registries, outcome research and decision support.
